## Data

- **Source:** Department of Tourism, [Philippine Tourism Data Dashboard](https://www.tourism.gov.ph/dot/data/), yearly files of monthly visitor arrivals (CC BY 4.0).
- **Break in classification:** the 2010–2021 files count arrivals by **country of residence**; the 2022 onward files count them by **country of citizenship**. The national monthly total is comparable across the break, so the models use only the total. The source market panel compares 2019 (residence) with the latest year (citizenship), so differences there are partly definitional. Markets with many overseas Filipinos or long-term residents are the most affected.
- **Pipeline:** `targets` reads every file in `data/raw/`, binds them, validates them, and writes `data/dot_arrivals_clean.csv` (national monthly total) and `data/dot_arrivals_by_market.csv`.

### Validation checks

```{r}
tar_read(validation)
```

## Counterfactual: what if COVID-19 had not happened?

The counterfactual model is trained only on January 2010 – February 2020 and projected forward. To pick it, three models were compared with rolling-origin cross-validation (training window grows one year at a time, 12-month-ahead forecasts):

```{r}
tar_read(cv_pre) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

Seasonal naive (each month = the same month a year earlier) is the benchmark: MASE is scaled against it, and a model is only worth using if it beats it. Here both ARIMA and ETS do, so the one with the lowest MASE is used: **`r attr(tar_read(cf_fit), "chosen")`** on log arrivals. The dashboard's recovery gap is the sum of (counterfactual − actual) from March 2020 to the latest month, computed across `r tar_read(cf_paths)$rep |> n_distinct()` simulated counterfactual paths, so it has an uncertainty interval.

## Measuring the shock: intervention model (ARIMAX)

An interrupted time-series model: a regression with ARIMA errors on log arrivals, fitted to the whole series, with four intervention terms:

| Term | Definition | Captures |
|---|---|---|
| `mar2020` | 1 in March 2020 | Partial first month of lockdown |
| `closed` | 1 from April 2020 to January 2022 | Border closure |
| `post` | 1 from February 2022 onward | Any lasting level shift after reopening |
| `gap_decay` | exp(−months since Feb 2022 / τ) from February 2022 | Post-reopening gap that shrinks over time |

All four are known for future months, so the model can also forecast. January 2022 was not collected by DOT; for this model only it is filled by log-linear interpolation between December 2021 and February 2022 (`r paste(attr(tar_read(inter_fit), "filled"), collapse = ", ")`). The decay speed τ was chosen by AICc:

```{r}
attr(tar_read(inter_fit), "tau_table") |> mutate(AICc = round(AICc, 1),
  chosen = tau_months == attr(tar_read(inter_fit), "tau"))
```

```{r}
#| class-output: model-report
cat(tar_read(inter_resid)$report, sep = "\n")
```

```{r}
co <- fabletools::tidy(tar_read(inter_fit))
eff <- function(term) {
  b <- co$estimate[co$term == term]; se <- co$std.error[co$term == term]
  sprintf("%s%% (95%% CI %s%% to %s%%)", round(100 * (exp(b) - 1), 1),
          round(100 * (exp(b - 1.96 * se) - 1), 1), round(100 * (exp(b + 1.96 * se) - 1), 1))
}
```

**Size of the shock.** While the borders were closed, arrivals were `r eff("closed")` relative to the level the model expects without the closure. The partial month of March 2020 was `r eff("mar2020")`.

## Forecasting: which model to trust?

Three forecasting approaches were compared on the same 12-month hold-out:

- **Naive Prophet**: the full series, with no knowledge of COVID.
- **Intervention ARIMA**: the model above, which carries forward the long-run 2010–2019 growth rate.
- **Post-reopening ARIMA**: an automatically selected ARIMA on log arrivals, fitted only to January 2023 onward, after the recovery ramp. A seasonal naive forecast (same month last year) is the benchmark.

### Hold-out test: last 12 months

Every model was refit without the last 12 months and scored on them:

```{r}
tar_read(holdout) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) |> arrange(MAPE)
```

The dashboard's headline forecast uses the **post-reopening ARIMA**. The intervention model assumes arrivals return to their pre-COVID growth rate; the hold-out test says that assumption has not held since 2023, so its forecast is shown for comparison only.

```{r}
#| class-output: model-report
cat(tar_read(recent_resid)$report, sep = "\n")
```

### Residual diagnostics

```{r}
bind_rows(tar_read(inter_resid)$ljung_box, tar_read(recent_resid)$ljung_box) |>
  transmute(model = .model, lags = lag, `Ljung-Box statistic` = round(lb_stat, 1),
            `p-value` = format.pval(lb_pvalue, digits = 2))
```

A p-value above 0.05 means no evidence of leftover autocorrelation. The intervention model fails this test: its residuals still have structure (the 2020–2022 period is hard to model as a few step changes), which is one more reason not to use it for the forecast.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.5
aug <- tar_read(recent_resid)$augment
acf_df <- with(stats::acf(aug$.innov, lag.max = 36, plot = FALSE, na.action = na.pass),
               tibble(lag = lag[-1], acf = acf[-1]))
conf <- 1.96 / sqrt(sum(!is.na(aug$.innov)))
ggplot(acf_df, aes(lag, acf)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-conf, conf), linetype = "dashed", colour = "#2563eb") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0)) +
  labs(x = "Lag (months)", y = "ACF", title = "Autocorrelation of residuals, post-reopening ARIMA") + theme_minimal()
```

## When will arrivals pass 2019?

Cumulative arrivals since 2020 can never catch up with the no-COVID path, so the target is the **rolling 12-month total** passing the **2019 calendar-year total** (`r num(tar_read(crossing)$target_2019_total, 0)`). This is checked on each of `r num(N_SIMS <- 1000, 0)` simulated future paths:

```{r}
bind_rows(`Post-reopening ARIMA (headline)` = tar_read(crossing),
          `Intervention ARIMA (sensitivity)` = tar_read(crossing_inter), .id = "model") |>
  mutate(prob_by_horizon = scales::percent(prob_by_horizon, 1))
```

`median_month` is shown only when at least half the paths pass 2019 by the horizon; `p90_month` only when at least 90% do.

## Cross-check: Bayesian structural time series

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.5
bsts_ci <- tar_read(causal)
if (is.null(bsts_ci)) {
  cat("The CausalImpact cross-check did not run in this build (package not installed or the fit failed; see the build log).")
} else ggplot(bsts_ci |> mutate(date = as.Date(date)), aes(date)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo95, ymax = hi95), fill = "grey80") +
  geom_line(aes(y = counterfactual), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(aes(y = actual)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Arrivals per month",
       title = "CausalImpact counterfactual (local trend + 12-month seasonality, log scale model)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

`CausalImpact` fits a Bayesian structural time series to the pre-COVID period and predicts the post-period. It's an independent check on the fable counterfactual; if the two disagree a lot, the gap estimate is fragile.

## Limitations

- No covariates: the counterfactual assumes the 2010–2019 trend would have continued. Exchange rates, airline capacity, the Boracay closure (April–October 2018) and visa policy aren't modelled.
- The classification change in 2022 affects source market comparisons, not the national total.
- The post-reopening model has only a few years of data (2023 onward), so its intervals widen quickly beyond 2027.
- 2022 figures come from a different system (One Health Pass) than 2010–2021 (arrival cards) and 2023 onward (Bureau of Immigration and eTravel).
- Forecast intervals assume the post-reopening pattern continues; a new shock would break them.
